title: What If Giant Insects Ruled the Skies Again?

scenes.text: What if giant insects ruled the skies again? You'd blame oxygen for stopping them. New research says no.
About 300 million years ago, oxygen made up roughly 35 percent of the air. Griffinflies, dragonfly relatives, had wingspans near 70 centimeters.
Insects have no lungs. Air enters through valves on their sides into tiny tubes that reach every cell, with air sacs working like bellows.
The old idea said extra oxygen let those tubes feed giants. But a study of 44 species found the tubes fill under one percent of flight muscle.
Across a size range of more than 10,000 times, tube space grew only 1.8 times. Air alone isn't the hard limit.
The likelier culprit may be predators. Birds and bats hunt flying insects today, and bigger insects are easier to catch.
